chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazzal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zurara, who said:

I and a group of our companions were traveling together, with Muyassar among them, between Mecca and Medina. We set out while we were uncertain about the time of midday (zawal). Some of us said to others, 'Walk with us a little until we are certain of the midday, then we will pray.' So we did, and we had not walked except a little until the caravan of Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) appeared to us. I said, 'The caravan has arrived.' I saw Muhammad ibn Ismail and said to him, 'Have you prayed?' He said to me, 'My grandfather instructed us, so we prayed Dhuhr and Asr together, then we set out.' I went to my companions and informed them of that.

key_terms.أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Abu Abdullah; a title for Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him).
key_terms.الزَّوَال: Midday; the time when the sun passes its zenith, marking the beginning of Dhuhr time.
key_terms.جَمِيعاً: Together; referring to the combination of two prayers into one time.
key_terms.قِطَار: Caravan; a group of travelers or a traveling party.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on combining Dhuhr and Asr prayers during travel according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the practical application of jam' al-salat (combining prayers) during travel, specifically illustrating the permissibility of combining Dhuhr and Asr when there is uncertainty regarding the precise time of zawal (midday). It underscores the authority of the Imams in clarifying ritual timings and demonstrates the flexibility granted to travelers in Shia jurisprudence to maintain prayer continuity without strict adherence to individual prayer times when conditions warrant. The narrative serves as a foundational evidence for the scholarly consensus on the validity of combining prayers under the pretext of travel or necessity.
